questions.stem: Christensen defines a disruptive innovation primarily by:
choices: How technologically radical it is.
The market trajectory it creates relative to mainstream customer needs.
Whether it is patented.
Whether it originated in a startup.
questions.explanation: Disruption is a market-trajectory concept, not a technology-radicalness concept. The disruptor enters below mainstream needs and improves faster than those needs rise.

questions.stem: Which is the best example of a low-end disruption?
choices: Tesla's Roadster
The original Kodak Brownie camera
Korean steel mini-mills attacking integrated steel mills
The iPhone
questions.explanation: Mini-mills entered at the lowest grade of steel (rebar), where integrated mills were happy to cede share, then climbed up the quality ladder. Textbook low-end disruption.

questions.stem: Which is the best example of a new-market disruption?
choices: Mobile money (M-Pesa) in East Africa reaching the unbanked
Faster Intel CPUs
Premium audio gear from Bose
Boeing's next-generation jetliner
questions.explanation: M-Pesa created a market among non-consumers of banking — a textbook new-market disruption.

questions.stem: Which statement is CORRECT about Tesla relative to Christensen's framework?
choices: Tesla is a textbook low-end disruption.
Tesla entered at the high end (Roadster, Model S) and moved down, so it does NOT fit Christensen's disruption pattern in the strict sense.
Tesla is a new-market disruption because EVs were a new category.
Tesla is sustaining innovation in the gas-engine market.
questions.explanation: Christensen himself argued Tesla is not a classic disruptor — it entered high-end and works down, the opposite of low-end disruption. A favourite exam nuance.

questions.stem: The 'innovator's dilemma' refers to the fact that:
choices: Innovators struggle to choose between competing technologies.
Well-managed incumbents fail to respond to disruption precisely because they listen to their best customers and chase the highest margins.
Startups cannot decide whether to bootstrap or raise capital.
Universities cannot decide whether to commercialise their research.
questions.explanation: The dilemma is that the practices that make incumbents successful (customer-listening, margin focus, big-market focus) are the same practices that blind them to disruption.

questions.stem: Performance overshoot in Christensen's model means:
choices: The disruptor's product overshoots the incumbent's at launch.
The incumbent improves its product faster than mainstream customers' needs rise, making the product 'too good' for many users.
The market grows faster than supply can meet.
Patents expire before the product becomes profitable.
questions.explanation: Performance overshoot opens the door to a disruptor: customers are paying for performance they no longer value, and a simpler/cheaper alternative becomes attractive.

questions.stem: Christensen's preferred organisational response for an incumbent facing disruption is to:
choices: Lower prices on the existing product line.
Spin out a separate autonomous unit with its own P&L, cost structure, and salesforce.
Acquire the disruptor and integrate it into the existing business.
Sue the disruptor for patent infringement.
questions.explanation: An autonomous unit can adopt the disruptor's cost structure and customer focus without being killed by the parent's resource-allocation immune system.

questions.stem: Which adopter category in Rogers' diffusion model makes up about 34% of the curve and is characterised by pragmatism and the need for references?
choices: Innovators
Early adopters
Early majority
Laggards
questions.explanation: Early majority (~34%) are pragmatists. They require proof, references, and standards before adopting. Moore's chasm sits just before this group.

questions.stem: Moore's 'chasm' in Crossing the Chasm refers to the gap between:
choices: Innovators and early adopters
Early adopters and early majority
Early majority and late majority
Late majority and laggards
questions.explanation: The chasm separates visionary early adopters from pragmatist early majority. Many disruptive products die in this gap.

questions.stem: Netflix's 1998 DVD-by-mail entry is best classified as:
choices: Sustaining innovation in the video rental market.
A disruption (mostly new-market plus some low-end on the convenience axis) relative to Blockbuster.
Process innovation only.
Position innovation only.
questions.explanation: DVD-by-mail created new consumption (long-tail catalogue) and undercut Blockbuster on the convenience axis (no late fees). Blockbuster's customers were not the target.

questions.stem: Why are MARGINS a structural reason incumbents fail to respond to disruptors?
choices: Incumbents cannot calculate margins accurately.
Disruptors target lower price points where the incumbent's margins look unattractive, so resource allocation goes elsewhere.
Margins on disruptive products are always higher than on incumbent products.
Tax law penalises low-margin businesses.
questions.explanation: The incumbent's CFO rationally favours high-margin investments. The disruptor's lower-margin opportunity loses every internal budget battle until it is too late.

questions.stem: Which of these is best classified as a SUSTAINING innovation?
choices: A new generation of jet engines making airliners 15% more fuel efficient.
Mobile money replacing bank accounts in East Africa.
Mini-mills replacing integrated steel mills.
Personal computers displacing mainframes.
questions.explanation: Better fuel efficiency improves the existing product on the dimension mainstream customers value. Incumbents (engine makers) typically win these battles.

questions.stem: Approximately what percentage of the population are 'innovators' in Rogers' diffusion model?
questions.explanation: Rogers' innovator share is ~2.5%. Early adopters ~13.5%, early/late majority ~34% each, laggards ~16%.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a reason incumbents fail to respond to disruption?
choices: Their best customers are not asking for the disruptor's product.
The disruptor's initial market is too small to justify investment.
Their salesforce is paid on commission and won't push the cheaper product.
Their R&D scientists are less talented than the disruptor's.
questions.explanation: Christensen's whole point is that incumbents fail despite having strong R&D and engineering. The failure is organisational/economic, not technical.

questions.stem: Uber's ride-hailing service is best classified as:
choices: Pure low-end disruption of taxis.
Mostly new-market (reaching people who would not have taken a taxi) with some low-end characteristics.
Sustaining innovation in the taxi industry.
Architectural innovation in dispatch systems.
questions.explanation: Christensen argued Uber created new ride-hailing demand among people who avoided taxis. Some price effect too, but the core is new-market expansion.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest signal that an industry is ripe for disruption?
choices: Performance overshoot: incumbents are improving faster than customers need.
Strong customer loyalty.
Heavy patent protection.
Low capital intensity.
questions.explanation: Overshoot creates a pool of over-served customers who would accept a worse-but-cheaper or simpler-and-more-convenient alternative. The disruption entry point.

questions.stem: The original Kodak Brownie camera (1900) is cited as a disruption because:
choices: It was the highest-quality camera available.
It created a mass market for photography among non-photographers who could not previously afford or operate cameras — a new-market disruption.
It used patented chemistry.
It was an architectural innovation in lens design.
questions.explanation: Brownies brought photography to ordinary people. Image quality was worse than professional cameras, but it reached non-consumers — a textbook new-market disruption.

questions.stem: Which is a defining characteristic of a sustaining innovation?
choices: It targets non-consumers.
It improves performance on the dimensions mainstream customers already value.
It is always low-margin.
It always originates outside the incumbent.
questions.explanation: Sustaining = better-on-existing-metrics. It does not have to be incremental — it can be radical (jet engines) — but it always improves on the dimensions mainstream customers value.

questions.stem: An incumbent acquires a disruptor and immediately integrates it into the parent business. Christensen would predict:
choices: Success: the disruptor benefits from the parent's resources.
Failure or stagnation: the parent's resource-allocation processes will starve the disruptor.
Indeterminate outcome with no theoretical guidance.
Success only if the disruptor's founders stay.
questions.explanation: Integration kills the disruptor's distinct cost structure, customer focus, and decision speed. Christensen recommends preserving autonomy.

questions.stem: On the performance-trajectory diagram, the moment when the disruptor's product crosses the mainstream-customer-need line is:
choices: The point at which the incumbent's response becomes possible.
The point at which the disruptor becomes 'good enough' for the mainstream and the incumbent rapidly loses share.
The point at which patents are filed.
The point at which the standards body intervenes.
questions.explanation: At the crossover, mainstream customers no longer need the incumbent's overshoot; they can buy the simpler, cheaper disruptor. Share shift accelerates.

questions.stem: Which feature does Rogers identify as the strongest predictor of adoption rate?
choices: Relative advantage over what is replaced.
Number of patents.
Marketing budget.
Government subsidies.
questions.explanation: Rogers' five attributes are relative advantage, compatibility, complexity, trialability, and observability. Relative advantage is the strongest single predictor.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a typical NEW-MARKET disruptor characteristic?
choices: It steals customers from the incumbent's best segment.
It targets non-consumers who previously had no money, no skill, or no access.
It immediately matches the incumbent on all performance dimensions.
It uses the incumbent's distribution channels.
questions.explanation: New-market disruption expands the total market into non-consumption. The incumbent does not initially lose share — but loses share later, when the disruptor improves.

questions.stem: Why is acquiring AND keeping autonomous a viable disruption response, while acquiring AND integrating typically is not?
choices: Integration triggers regulatory review.
Autonomy preserves the disruptor's distinct cost structure, customer focus, and decision-making — integration imposes the incumbent's incompatible processes.
Autonomous units are tax-advantaged.
Integration violates Christensen's theorem.
questions.explanation: The whole point of the spin-out logic. Once integrated, the parent's resource-allocation processes apply, and the disruptor reverts to incumbent behaviour.

questions.stem: Christensen's framework is sometimes criticised because:
choices: It is too narrowly applied — many cases labelled 'disruption' do not actually fit the model.
It only applies to manufacturing.
It contradicts the Utterback-Abernathy model.
It ignores process innovation.
questions.explanation: The term 'disruption' is widely abused. Christensen and successors have pushed back on calling every successful startup a Christensen disruptor (e.g. Uber, Tesla edge cases).

questions.stem: A budget airline (Ryanair, Southwest) attacking full-service carriers is best classified as:
choices: Sustaining innovation.
Low-end disruption — accepting worse performance on amenities for far lower price, eventually moving upmarket.
Pure new-market disruption.
Architectural innovation.
questions.explanation: Budget carriers attacked the price-sensitive low end. Full-service carriers initially ceded the segment, then lost share even on profitable routes as budget carriers added features.
